headline: Bunker on the Reef, Bass in the Dark: Montauk's August Turn
subhead: The Point's gone quiet on top and loud underneath — bunker pods thick off the Lighthouse, blues crashing them in daylight, bass working the boulders after the sun drops.
body_markdown:
This is the stretch of the season where Montauk asks you to be patient, and if you've fished the Point long enough you know that patience here always gets paid back with interest come September. Right now we're sitting in that in-between water — surface temps off the Lighthouse holding around 74, 75 degrees, warm enough to push the big resident bass off the top and into their summer pattern: deep, tight to structure, and mostly nocturnal. That's not a knock on the fishing. That's just what forty years on this rock has taught me happens every August, and this year is following the script.

The boulder field off the Lighthouse is still the epicenter, but you've got to fish it different than you did in June. I've been working the incoming tide starting about two hours before the top, easing bunker chunks and whole eels down into the pockets between the rocks, letting the current do the work. Rich guys will tell you they're catching bass in broad daylight off the rocks right now — I'd be careful trusting that unless it's overcast and the tide is really honking. My best fish this past week, a mid-30s bass that took a live eel fished on a fish-finder rig in maybe 15 feet of water, came at 11 p.m. on the building tide, right in that seam where North Bar's current wraps around and meets the deeper water off the Point. That's the program right now — go after dark, fish the current edges, and don't expect it to be fast. Two, three quality bites a tide is a good night this time of year.

What's not subtle at all is the bluefish. Bunker pods have been thick off Shagwong Reef and out past the Point, and the blues have been all over them in full daylight — the kind of surface chop and diving gulls that'll pull every boat within five miles off its anchor. Bucktails, poppers, anything chrome thrown into the melee will get bit, and these aren't snappers — we're talking three, four, five-pound cocktail blues with some genuine slammers mixed in. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the peanut bunker would keep spreading and that back-bay blues would spike as a result — and that's exactly what's playing out now. Fort Pond Bay has peanut bunker stacked at the east end creek mouth, and the cocktail blues have followed them in on the incoming tide. Small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster — worked fast through the froth is all you need there, and it's a great spot to bring a kid or a first-timer because the action is nonstop even when the Point bite goes quiet.

Weakfish are trickling into that same bunker pattern. Lake Montauk, particularly around the Star Island jetty on the outgoing tide when the harbor drains hard through the inlet channel, has been giving up weakfish in the two-to-four-pound class to guys drifting bucktails tipped with a strip of squid along the current seam. It's not a blitz — one or two fish an outgoing tide if you put in the time — but weakfish in Montauk waters always feel like a bonus, and with bunker thick in the bay right now I expect that bite to hold through the rest of the month.

Fluke have slid off the shallow flats and settled onto the deeper structure, which is normal for August. I've had the most consistent action drifting the drop-offs around Frisco Rock and the deeper edges off Shagwong in 35 to 50 feet, 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, working the drift slow and staying in contact with bottom. Fish aren't huge — most going 16 to 19 inches — but there are keepers mixed in, and porgies have been riding shotgun on the same drifts. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod, anchor up on the reef structure off the harbor mouth and soak sandworms or clam on the bottom for porgies — that bite has been steady and reliable all week, no drama, just consistent pulls.

Now here's what I'm watching closest heading into next week. Water's sitting right at that threshold temperature where false albacore and bonito start showing around the rips — we're not there yet with confirmed fish, but the ingredients are lining up: warm water pushing out of the Sound, bait getting pressured into tight balls off the Point, and that first cool night or two of building current that usually flips the switch. I've seen this pattern plenty of Augusts — the water creeps into the mid-70s, everybody starts talking about it at the dock, and then one morning somebody's hooked up to something that peels drag like nothing else in the striper zone. If I had to bet, I'd say the first confirmed albie or bonito shows up east of the Point or out toward Shagwong within the next week to ten days, especially if this stable weather holds. Until then, my time's going into the night bass bite at the boulders and the reliable daytime action on blues and porgies — proven fish over speculative ones, every time, until the calendar tells me otherwise.
